lessons.title: AI for school and side jobs: using ChatGPT and Gemini smartly

steps.title: AI as a study buddy, not a replacement
steps.body: ChatGPT and Gemini are strong at: drafting first versions, summarizing, brainstorming, checking code, improving a cover letter. Think of it as a classmate who always has time — not a replacement for your own knowledge and judgment.

steps.title: Plagiarism and AI detection: why this can cost you your degree
steps.body: Having AI write an entire assignment or thesis and submitting it as your own work is fraud — schools and universities increasingly use AI-detection tools, and the consequences (suspension, invalidated grade) are serious. Use AI to learn and structure your work, not to skip doing your own.

steps.title: Always double-check AI output
steps.body: Using AI for an assignment, application, or side job? Always verify facts, numbers, and citations yourself before submitting or sending — an AI can sound convincing while being factually wrong (sometimes called 'hallucinating').

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Try asking Gemini below to draft a cover letter for a side job or internship, and critically judge whether the answer is accurate and sounds like you.

steps.title: Working iteratively
steps.body: Don't expect the perfect answer right away. Follow up with 'Make it shorter', 'Use a more casual tone', 'Add an example'. This back-and-forth often gets a better result than trying to write one perfect prompt.

steps.title: Role prompts
steps.body: Give the AI a role: 'Respond as an experienced recruiter and give feedback on my resume' or 'Explain this as if I just started this subject'. This shapes the tone and level of detail in the answer.

steps.title: Reusing templates
steps.body: Often working on similar tasks (like summaries for school)? Save a prompt that works well as a template, so you can reuse it instead of starting from scratch every time.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Try a role prompt below: ask Gemini to respond as a specific expert on a topic you're interested in.

steps.title: What an AI company does with your data
steps.body: By default, what you type in an AI chat can be used to train the model. Check the settings (in ChatGPT for example: Settings > Data controls) to turn this off if you don't want that.

steps.title: Deepfakes: a personal risk for you too
steps.body: AI can create convincing fake video, audio, and even fake photos of real people — including explicit fake images ('deepfake nudes') of someone without their consent. This is illegal and can cause serious harm. Be skeptical of voice messages or videos that pressure you to act, and know that you can always report misuse of your own likeness to the police.

steps.title: What you never share with an AI chatbot
steps.body:
• Passwords, DigiD details, national ID numbers
  • Confidential info from your job or internship without authorization
  • Medical or financial data belonging to other people
  • Photos of official documents (passport, driver's license, student ID)

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Check in your own AI account (ChatGPT or Gemini) whether you can opt out of your conversations being used to train the model.

lessons.title: AI ethics: bias, copyright, and when not to use it

steps.title: Bias in AI
steps.body: AI models are trained on existing data from the world — including existing biases. In sensitive applications (like resume screening or study advice), this can lead to unfair outcomes. Use AI here as, at most, a helper tool — never as the sole decision-maker.

steps.title: Copyright: who actually owns an AI image?
steps.body: Using AI to create images, music, or text for social media, a portfolio, or an assignment? Be aware that copyright law around AI content is still evolving, and that some AI tools are trained on material (art, music) whose creators never gave consent. Check your school's or client's policy if you're unsure.

steps.title: When NOT to use AI
steps.body: Not for: medical, legal, or financial advice without consulting an expert; official decisions; anything where a mistake has serious consequences (like your student finance or a contract). Treat AI as a sparring partner, not the one ultimately responsible.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think of a situation from your own studies, side job, or life where you would use AI, and one where you would deliberately choose not to. What's the difference?
